text: Take a position. In class, you have to take a position.
Stakeholder. The clients are the most important stakeholders.
Cut costs. If we cut costs, we would lose good people.
In the long run. In the long run, the bank would be stronger.
Risky. It is risky, but I would do it.
Gut feeling. My gut feeling says no.
Devil's advocate. Let me play devil's advocate for a minute.
Back up. Can you back it up with a number?
David, the bank has three hundred branches and it is losing money. If you were the CEO, what would you do?
Well, it depends.
It always depends. I want you to take a position.
OK. If I were the CEO, I would close sixty branches.
Sixty? That sounds risky.
I can back it up. Those branches have fewer than ten clients a day.
Let me play devil’s advocate. If you closed them, you would lose those clients.
Some of them, yes. But most of them already use the app.
And the people who work there? They are stakeholders too.
Fair point. I wouldn’t fire them. I would move them to the call center. In the long run, the bank would be stronger.
If I were the CEO, I would close sixty branches.
I can back it up with one number.
It is risky, but in the long run it would work.
Fair point, but the clients are the most important stakeholders.
If I were you, I wouldn't wait.

Welcome to the case method. In this room, I will not give you the answer. I will ask you a question, and the question is always the same: if you were the CEO, what would you do? There is no right answer, but there is a wrong one. The wrong answer is, it depends. Of course it depends. Everything depends. I want you to take a position. Say, if I were the CEO, I would close the factory, and then back it up with one number. If a classmate plays devil's advocate, good. Listen, and answer. If you changed your mind every time someone pushed back, you would never decide anything. And a CEO who never decides is not a CEO.

On my third day, the professor looked at me and asked, what would you do if you were the CEO of this airline? My gut feeling said, do not cut costs, protect the service. But I was afraid. So I said, it depends. The professor smiled and waited. So I tried again. I said, if I were the CEO, I would not cut costs this year. In the long run, the airline would lose its best clients. Then a classmate played devil's advocate. He said, but the airline is losing money now. I said, fair point, but the stakeholders who matter most are the clients. Nobody agreed with me. And that was fine. The professor wrote my name on the board.
